page6_img_2.png.title: Monthly reviews trend for Bing (adoption) and Office (release cycle)
page6_img_2.png.description: Scatter plot of monthly review counts (y-axis labeled “Reviews”) over time (x-axis labeled “Month”), with blue squares for Bing and red triangles for Office. Bing’s points show a steady, monotonic increase from a low baseline toward higher monthly review counts, illustrating tool adoption and growing review activity. Office shows a rapid rise to a pronounced mid-period peak followed by a clear decline in later months, consistent with a release-driven cyclic pattern; at its peak Office exceeds Bing, but Office activity falls off near release. Exact numeric values and dates are omitted for confidentiality, so the plot should be read for relative trends rather than precise counts.

page7_img_1.png.title: Violin plots of lines changed per review across projects (log scale)
page7_img_1.png.description: A set of violin (bean) plots showing the distribution of lines changed per review for six projects (Android, Chrome, AMD, Bing, Office, SQL) with the y-axis on a logarithmic scale and a horizontal bar marking the median for each project. Android and AMD have similar median change sizes (about 44 lines), Chrome’s median is larger (about 78 lines and typically spans ~5 files), while the industrial projects Bing, Office, and SQL have still larger medians (roughly 120–150 lines). All distributions are left-skewed with long right tails, indicating most reviews are small but some reviews involve much larger churn; even so, these medians remain substantially below the traditional Lucent inspection median (~263 lines) reported in the paper.

page8_img_1.png.title: Boxplots of comments per review across projects (log scale)
page8_img_1.png.description: Boxplots (y-axis on a log scale) compare the distribution of comments per review for five projects (Android, Chrome, Bing, Office, SQL). Median comment counts reported in the paper are about 3 for Android and Office and about 4 for Chrome and Bing (SQL reported as 3); all projects show right-skewed distributions with moderate IQRs and many high-value outliers (some reviews have hundreds to over a thousand comments). Because contemporary review tools do not record explicit defect counts, the authors treat the number of comments as an upper-bound proxy for review-discussed issues, and the similar median levels across projects indicate comparable amounts of review discussion in both open-source and industrial settings.

page7_img_2.png.title: Reviewers per review by project (log-scale boxplots)
page7_img_2.png.description: Boxplots (y-axis on a log scale) compare the number of reviewers who actively participate in each review for six projects: Android, Chrome, AMD, Bing, Office, and SQL. The bold median line in every box sits at two reviewers, indicating a consistent central tendency of two participants per review across projects. All projects show long right-hand tails and many outlier points (individual reviews) that involve substantially more reviewers—particularly Office and SQL, which have the largest extreme values—illustrating occasional high-participation reviews. This plot visually supports the paper’s finding that two reviewers are typical while additional reviewers are invited in higher-risk or complex cases.

page6_img_1.png.title: Reviews per month by project (log-scale violin plots)
page6_img_1.png.description: Violin plots (logarithmic y-axis from 1 to 10,000) compare the monthly distribution of code reviews for six projects (left to right: Android, Chrome, AMD, Bing, Office, SQL). Horizontal bars inside each violin mark the median review count; as reported in the paper, median values are low for Android (~310 reviews/month) and modest for AMD (hundreds, rising after adoption), intermediate for Chrome (~1,576) and Bing (~2,290), and highest for SQL (~3,739) and Office (~4,384). The shapes show long tails and differing spread: some projects (e.g., Office, Bing, AMD) exhibit wide variability or long upper tails consistent with adoption or cyclic activity, while Chrome and SQL show relatively concentrated, stable monthly review volumes.

page5_img_1.png.title: Distribution of review first‑response and full‑interval times by project
page5_img_1.png.description: This bean/violin plot shows, for each project (Android, Chrome, AMD, Bing, Office, SQL), two distributions on a log‑scaled y‑axis in days: the time to first response (left violin; AMD lacks first‑response data) and the full review completion interval (right violin). Medians for full intervals reported in the paper are roughly on the order of hours to a day (Chrome ~15.7 h, Android ~20.8 h, AMD ~17.5 h, Bing ~14.7 h, Office ~18.9 h, SQL ~19.8 h), while first responses are typically shorter (most picked up within a few hours). The violins show most review activity concentrated at short intervals but with long right tails — occasional reviews take many days — highlighting that reviews are generally quick and frequent but have outliers of much longer duration.

page9_img_1.png.title: Quartile summary of comments, threads, and resolved threads per review (Bing, Office, SQL)
page9_img_1.png.description: Table of 1st quartile, median, and 3rd quartile values for three review activity measures (Comments, Threads, Resolved) for Bing, Office, and SQL. Medians show modest discussion per review: Comments = 4 (Bing), 3 (Office), 3 (SQL); Threads = 2 (Bing), 2 (Office), 3 (SQL); Resolved = 0 for all three (i.e., at least half of reviews have no thread marked resolved). Lower quartiles are consistently 2 comments / 1 thread / 0 resolved, while upper quartiles indicate heavier discussion in some reviews (up to 9 comments & 6 threads for Bing; 8 comments & 5 threads for Office; 8 comments & 7 threads for SQL). In the paper’s context these counts are presented as implicit, non‑intrusive proxies for defects and show that most reviews generate discussion but relatively few threads are formally marked resolved in the typical case.

page10_img_1.png.title: Files seen per developer by project (submitted vs total)
page10_img_1.png.description: Split violin plots for Android, Chrome, Bing, Office, and SQL compare the distribution of distinct files a developer has submitted (dark left half) versus the total files they know about after reviewing (light right half). The vertical axis is log-scaled (number of files) and each half-violin shows the full distribution with a horizontal line marking the median. For example, a median Chrome developer submits to 24 files, reviews 38, and thus knows about 43 files; across projects review increases the median developer’s known files by roughly 66% (Android) up to 150% (SQL), with Bing and Office showing about 100% and 122% increases respectively. The plots also show Android’s heavy concentration of “drive-by” contributors (many developers who submitted fewer than five files) and that, in every project, the total-known distribution (right halves) lies above the submitted-only distribution, indicating substantial knowledge spread via review (data excludes submissions/reviews with >10 files).

page8_img_2.png.title: Boxplots of resubmissions per review (log scale) by project
page8_img_2.png.description: The figure shows boxplots (y-axis on a log scale) of the number of times a change is resubmitted during review for five projects: Android, Chrome, Bing, Office, and SQL. In the median case most reviews have only 1–2 submissions (Android and Office around 1; Chrome, Bing, and SQL around 2), while the distributions are right-skewed with many outliers — some reviews see dozens of resubmissions. This indicates that contemporary reviews typically require only a small number of iterative fix-and-resubmit cycles, though a minority of reviews undergo many more iterations.

page2_img_table_1.png.title: Project datasets: study period, duration, and number of reviews
page2_img_table_1.png.description: A tabular summary of the projects used in the study, showing for each project the calendar period examined, the duration in years, and the total number of reviews collected. Microsoft projects dominate the largest datasets (MS Bing: 2010–2013, 3.7 years, 102K reviews; MS Office 2013: 2011–2013, 2.7 years, 96K; MS SQL Server: 2011–2013, 2.8 years, 80K). Open-source projects range from tens of thousands of reviews (FreeBSD: 1995–2006, 12.0 years, 47K; Linux: 2005–2008, 3.5 years, 28K; KDE: 2002–2008, 5.6 years, 23K) down to smaller OSS sets (Apache, Subversion, Android, Chrome OS). The traditional Lucent inspection dataset is much smaller (1994–1995, 1.5 years, 88 reviews), illustrating the wide variation in dataset size and study span across projects.
